To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the F286Y mutation tempers the signal‐sequence suppressor phenotype of PrlA by reducing the SecY‐SecA binding affinity.

SecYEG with the PrlA4 double mutation F286Y/I408N exhibits an intermediate SecA binding affinity between wild‐type SecYEG and the SecY(I408) mutant, and that the translocation of the PrlA1 and PrlA2 preproteins is reduced compared to wild‐type SecYEg.

the F286Y mutation in PrlA4, a double mutant of the SecY subunit of the translocon, reduces the SecA binding and translocation activity of the translocons, and that this effect correlates with the reduced SecA binding and ATPase activities of the F286Y mutant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of preprotein translocation across the Escherichiacoli membrane.
the identification of the structural elements of the translocon that determine the signal sequence requirement for preprotein translocation.
the molecular mechanism of the prl phenotype of PrlA and the effect of the F286Y mutation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prl phenotype of PrlA is due to the I408N substitution.
PrlA4 has two independent effects, namely, a strong prl phenotype and an elevated SecA affinity that both depend on the individual mutations.
the F286Y mutation in PrlA4 reduces the signal sequence suppressive activity of the I408 mutation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prl phenotype is a result of a reduced SecA binding affinity and that this is a consequence of the loss of the conserved aromatic residue at position 286 in the SecY protein.
the prl phenotype is caused by the combination of a reduced SecA binding affinity of the mutated SecY and a higher affinity for the preprotein substrate.
the prl phenotype of PrlA is caused by the I408N and F286Y mutations of SecY that increase and reduce the SecA binding affinities, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the prl phenotype can be separated into two independent components: the increased translocation efficiency of preproteines with a defective signal sequence, and the increased translocation rate of preproteine with a normal signal sequence.
the prl phenotype is not a simple consequence of the increased SecA binding affinity of SecY.
the SecA‐binding affinity is the most relevant determinant of the prl phenotype.
